options.rationale: The forecast answers the question about the future without altering the record of what was committed, which is why both figures can coexist without contradiction.

options.text: a re-baselined schedule reissued with the eight days absorbed into the remaining work
options.rationale: Not used. Re-baselining to make a variance disappear destroys the only record of how the project has performed, and leaves the next slippage with nothing to be measured against.

questions.explanation: A baseline and a forecast answer different questions and both are needed at once: one is the fixed reference that makes variance meaningful, the other is the current best expectation of the outcome. Reporting a slipped project by moving the baseline collapses the two, so the project appears to be on plan while nobody can see how far it has drifted. Re-baselining is legitimate when the agreement itself has changed, and not as a way of tidying away a variance.
questions.mindset: Hold the baseline still so the forecast has something to mean.

questions.stem: A new sponsor joins your water treatment upgrade in month five. Having watched the software workstream demonstrate something every fortnight, she asks that the plant workstream move to two-week iterations as well, saying the contrast between the two makes the hardware side look slow. Pump lead times are sixteen weeks and commissioning cannot be reversed once started. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Show her where iterating would genuinely help on the plant side and where lead times and irreversibility prevent it, and propose changes only where the constraints allow.
options.rationale: It takes the sponsor's underlying concern about visibility seriously while keeping the approach tied to what the work will actually support, and it names which parts can move.

options.text: Move both workstreams to two-week iterations as requested, since the sponsor owns the delivery approach.
options.rationale: It applies a cadence to work whose uncertainty and lead times do not support it, on the strength of a preference rather than a constraint, and the cadence will be theatre within a month.

options.text: Explain that physical works cannot be delivered iteratively and keep the plant workstream as it is.
options.rationale: It defends the current approach as a category rule, and gives up the parts of the plant work — prototyping, staged commissioning, early factory tests — where iteration genuinely does apply.

options.text: Report the plant workstream on a fortnightly cycle to match the software team, leaving the work itself unchanged.
options.rationale: It gives the sponsor the appearance of the change she asked for, which costs more trust when noticed than declining would have cost in the first place.

questions.explanation: Delivery approach follows the constraints of the work — how quickly feedback can be obtained, how reversible decisions are, and what lead times apply — rather than the preference of whoever is watching. Where a request cannot be met as stated, the useful response separates the concern behind it from the mechanism proposed, since visibility and cadence are different things and only one of them was actually being asked for. On mixed programmes the honest answer to 'can this be iterative' is usually that some of it can.
questions.mindset: Let the constraints of the work choose the approach, and answer 'partly' when that is the truthful answer.

questions.stem: Your veterinary practice software product owner has ordered the backlog strictly by value. Three of the top five items each need the same clinical data specialist, who is available for one week in the next six because she is committed to a regulatory audit. The team is about to plan the next iteration and intends to work down the order as written. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the near-term order revisited so that value and feasibility are weighed together, and the specialist's one week is spent on whichever item most needs her.
options.rationale: Order should reflect what can actually be started as well as what is worth most, and a scarce week is best spent where the specialist is genuinely irreplaceable.

options.text: Keep the value order intact and let the team work around the specialist's availability as they go.
options.rationale: It treats the backlog order as untouchable and pushes an unresolvable dependency into the iteration, where it becomes blocked work rather than a planning choice.

options.text: Schedule all three items into the specialist's available week.
options.rationale: It fills a scarce week without asking whether all three genuinely need her or whether one does and the others merely benefit.

options.text: Ask the product owner to lower the priority of two of the three items.
options.rationale: It asks for a value judgement to be misstated in order to accommodate a capacity constraint, which corrupts the one signal the order is supposed to carry.

questions.explanation: Backlog order expresses what is worth most, but the sequence a team actually works in also has to respect what can be started, and the two are reconciled in the near-term ordering rather than by pretending one of them does not exist. Where a constraint is a scarce person, the useful question is which item genuinely requires that person rather than which would merely go faster with them. Rewriting priorities to disguise a constraint destroys the meaning of the order for everyone downstream.
questions.mindset: Order by value, then sequence by what can actually be started, without pretending either consideration is the other.

questions.stem: Your programme must choose between two data migration tools. The pilot that will distinguish them reports in week 9. Whichever is chosen needs licences and trained operators, and the supplier quotes a six-week lead time from order. Migration build starts in week 16 and cannot begin without the tool in place. The timeline marks four candidate positions for the decision point. Select the position where it belongs.

graphic.title: Twenty-week timeline showing the pilot reporting in week 9, a six-week supplier lead time and migration build starting in week 16, with four candidate decision positions
graphic.caption: Select a candidate position. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Week 0 — at plan approval, alongside the other baseline decisions
regions.rationale: It settles the question before any evidence exists, purely to have it settled. Deciding early is only a virtue when waiting would cost more than the information is worth, and here the pilot is already funded.

regions.label: Week 6 — while the pilot is still running, to protect the lead time
regions.rationale: It pays for the pilot and then declines to use it. Deciding three weeks before the results arrive discards the very information the pilot was commissioned to produce.

regions.label: Week 10 — after the pilot reports, with six weeks left before build
regions.rationale: The pilot has reported and exactly the quoted lead time remains before build starts. This is the last point at which the decision can use all the evidence and still be delivered in time.

regions.label: Week 16 — at the start of migration build, once the need is immediate
regions.rationale: It waits until the decision is unavoidable, by which point the six-week lead time guarantees the build starts six weeks late whichever tool is chosen.

questions.explanation: A decision that depends on both incoming evidence and an outgoing lead time has a window rather than a date, and the window opens when the evidence arrives and closes a lead time before the result is needed. Planning the decision at the closing edge preserves every option for as long as possible without putting the dependent work at risk. Deciding before the window opens wastes the evidence, and letting it close converts a choice into a delay.
questions.mindset: Place a decision at the last point where it can still use the evidence and still be acted on in time.

questions.stem: Your bottom-up estimate for a museum's collection management replacement totals €1.14 million against an approved budget of €900,000. The finance business partner has asked you to go back to the workstream leads and sharpen the numbers, noting that estimates always contain padding and that a submission over budget will not be considered by the investment committee. The scope has not changed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the estimate as given and present the scope that could be removed or deferred to reach €900,000, with the consequence of each reduction.
options.rationale: It keeps the estimate as evidence and moves the only variable that can honestly move, while giving the committee a decision it is equipped to take.

options.text: Reduce the contingency provision until the total comes within the approved budget.
options.rationale: It closes a scope gap with money set aside for uncertainty, so the first thing that goes wrong reopens the same gap with no provision left.

options.text: Ask the workstream leads to re-estimate with the €900,000 target in mind.
options.rationale: It anchors the estimate to the desired answer, producing a number that satisfies the committee and predicts nothing, and it teaches the leads that estimates are negotiable downwards.

options.text: Submit the full estimate with an explanation and leave the shortfall for the committee to resolve.
options.rationale: It is honest and stops one step short. Presenting the problem without the options leaves the committee to invent scope reductions it is far less well placed to design.

questions.explanation: An estimate is evidence about what work will cost, and a budget is a decision about what the organisation will spend, so a gap between them is resolved by changing the work rather than the evidence. Adjusting estimates to fit a target destroys their value as a forecast and their usefulness as a control, and it usually reappears as an overrun that nobody predicted because the prediction was suppressed. Presenting the options alongside the gap is what turns bad news into a decision.
questions.mindset: Move the scope to reach a budget, never the estimate, and bring the options with the gap.

questions.stem: Your logistics product is built by one team split across Manila, Lisbon and Chicago, with a single hour in which all three are at work. Planning currently happens in that hour and routinely overruns without concluding, and work is allocated to whoever is free rather than by location. Cross-location handoffs regularly wait a full day for an answer. The team is well regarded and morale is dropping. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Restructure the work so each location owns whole slices with few cross-location dependencies, and plan the dependencies that remain into the overlap hour.
options.rationale: It reduces the amount of coordination the day needs rather than trying to fit more coordination into an hour that cannot grow.

options.text: Move planning decisions into a written asynchronous form with a fixed deadline for objections, keeping the overlap hour for what genuinely needs live conversation.
options.rationale: Most planning input does not require simultaneity, and a stated deadline is what stops asynchronous discussion from drifting instead of deciding.

options.text: Rotate the planning meeting time so that each location takes its turn attending outside working hours.
options.rationale: It distributes the pain evenly and leaves the structural dependency untouched. Fairness about who suffers is not a substitute for reducing the need to meet.

options.text: Have the project manager take the planning decisions between iterations and communicate them to the three locations.
options.rationale: It buys speed by removing the people who hold the information from the decision, and the resulting plans will be revised as soon as they meet reality.

options.text: Split into three independent teams with separate backlogs, each free to plan on its own.
options.rationale: It solves coordination by abandoning it, and one product with three unaligned backlogs becomes three products that have to be reintegrated later.

questions.explanation: When coordination capacity is fixed by geography, the durable response is to design the work so less coordination is required, and only then to make the remaining coordination efficient. Allocating work by availability rather than by location maximises the handoffs that the time zones make expensive, so it is the allocation rule that needs changing first. Measures that redistribute inconvenience, or that centralise decisions to avoid the conversation, leave the underlying dependency structure exactly as it was.
questions.mindset: Reduce the coordination the work demands before optimising the coordination you can afford.

questions.stem: You inherit a programme whose six workstreams were baselined one at a time as each completed planning, across five months. The integrated plan is a roll-up of the six. Comparing them, you find three assume a three-day cutover weekend in October and three assume five days, and the resource assumptions behind two of them were written before a hiring freeze that the later four accounted for. The board believes it has one approved plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reconcile the conflicting assumptions first, then establish a single integrated baseline at one date, and report the variance that reconciliation exposes against the original commitments.
options.rationale: The assumptions have to agree before a baseline means anything, and taking the whole programme to one date is what turns six documents into a plan. The exposed variance is a real finding, not a failure to be smoothed away.

options.text: Keep the six baselines and reconcile them each month in reporting so that the board sees a consistent view.
options.rationale: It preserves the appearance of stability by paying a reconciliation cost every month forever, while the underlying assumptions continue to disagree and drive incompatible decisions.

options.text: Re-baseline everything to the current integrated forecast, so that the programme starts from a consistent and achievable position.
options.rationale: It achieves consistency by erasing five months of performance history, leaving the board with a plan that agrees with itself and nothing to measure the programme against.

options.text: Baseline the October cutover jointly across all six workstreams and leave each workstream's other assumptions as they are.
options.rationale: It fixes the collision that happens to be visible and leaves the resource assumptions, written either side of a hiring freeze, to produce the next one unannounced.

questions.explanation: A set of separately approved plans is not an integrated plan, because integration is precisely the reconciliation of assumptions that the individual plans were free to make independently. Baselining component by component over months guarantees that early components encode conditions the later ones know to be false. Correcting it means agreeing the shared assumptions, setting one baseline at one moment, and reporting honestly on the gap that appears — the gap was always there and was merely undiscoverable.
questions.mindset: One plan means one set of reconciled assumptions baselined at one moment; anything else is several plans under a cover sheet.
